flashcards.q: What are the two independent kernel mechanisms containers are built from?
flashcards.a: Namespaces (visibility isolation — what a process can see) and cgroups (resource isolation — what a process can use). No container-specific kernel object exists.
pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time (time is newest, kernel 5.6, 2020).

flashcards.q: Why does the user namespace matter most for container-escape severity?
flashcards.a: It maps UID 0 inside the container to an unprivileged UID on the host, so even an escape doesn't automatically grant host root — not mapping host root into the container blocks the most severe escape class.

flashcards.q: Why do CPU limits throttle but memory limits kill?
flashcards.a: CPU is compressible (kernel just stops scheduling for the rest of the cfs_quota_us period, default period 100ms). Memory is incompressible — crossing memory.max triggers immediate SIGKILL via the OOM killer.

flashcards.q: What does container exit code 137 mean?
flashcards.a: 128 + 9 (SIGKILL) — the signature of an OOM kill from exceeding memory.max, not an application-level crash.

flashcards.q: What CPU-throttling ratio in production signals a limit set too tight?
flashcards.a: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total above roughly 25% on a normal traffic day.

flashcards.q: What is the process chain from `docker run` to a running container?
flashcards.a: docker CLI -> dockerd -> containerd (lifecycle mgmt) -> containerd-shim (1 per container, survives containerd restarts, holds stdio) -> runc (OCI runtime, does clone()/unshare() + cgroup writes, execs, then exits).

flashcards.q: Why does runc exit right after starting the container instead of staying resident?
flashcards.a: So restarting/upgrading a long-lived daemon (containerd/dockerd) doesn't require killing running containers — the shim, not runc, is the container's real parent process.

flashcards.q: What causes the OverlayFS 'slow first write' surprise?
flashcards.a: Modifying a file that exists only in a read-only lower image layer triggers a full copy-up of the entire file into the writable upper layer before the write proceeds.

flashcards.q: Why is a container escape generally more severe than a VM escape?
flashcards.a: A container shares the host kernel with no hypervisor boundary, so escaping the namespace/cgroup jail lands directly in host kernel context; a VM escape must additionally defeat a hardware-enforced hypervisor boundary.

flashcards.q: Name a real recent runc container-escape CVE and its mechanism.
flashcards.a: CVE-2024-21626 (runc <=1.1.11): an internal file descriptor leak could give a newly-spawned container process a working directory in the host filesystem namespace, granting full host filesystem access.
A fork bomb inside one container exhausting the host's entire PID table, which would affect every other process on the host, not just the offending container.

flashcards.q: What changed between cgroups v1 and v2?
flashcards.a: v1 had separate per-controller hierarchies with unreliable buffered-I/O accounting; v2 (kernel 4.5, 2016) unifies everything into one hierarchy with more consistent accounting. Migration across production is still ongoing.

flashcards.q: What's the production alternative to plain containers for running untrusted, multi-tenant code?
flashcards.a: gVisor (userspace syscall interception) or Kata Containers (per-job lightweight VM with its own guest kernel) — both trade overhead for a stronger isolation boundary than shared-kernel namespaces/cgroups.
